extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, corporate communications managers, PR students and practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for practitioners who plan, execute, and ethically advise on campaigns to shape public opinion using media, events, research, and group-targeted messaging. Emphasizes methods, audience segmentation, media use, and ethical obligations of PR counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret client to public and public to client
rubrics_metrics.description: "He interprets the client to the public, which he is enabled to do in part because he interprets the public to the client."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel directs and supervises client activities wherever they impinge on the public; gives advice on all occasions the client appears before the public (concrete or idea); advises use of any medium—printed, spoken, visualized word (advertising, lectures, stage, pulpit, newspaper, photograph, wireless, mail, etc.). Examples: advising a hotel to renew a famous maître d’hôtel to counter a rumor; advising magazines how to reuse editorial material to reach other influential publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: "The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on newspapers, radio, motion pictures, mail, lectures, advertising, professional journals, photographs, wires and other established channels. Choose the medium(s) most appropriate to the target group; create releasable news items suited to those media (e.g., press services, wire dispatches, supplied abstracts). Examples include Associated Press dispatch about employment, radio inaugurations between cities, motion-picture and photographic coverage of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and target publics (audience segmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the public into groups by geography, profession, business, religion, economic position, preferences and other criteria; "This classification of his public into the right groups for the proper appeals is one of the most important functions of the public relations counsel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct segmentation before selecting appeals; prepare tailored materials for each group (e.g., ethnic, professional, hobbyist angles). Use direct mail, targeted press, and specialized media to reach segments. Example: Lithuania campaign produced different materials for ethnologists, language students, jewelers, sporting fans, and senators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor content to the interests of each audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Make material relevant to specific audiences by translating facts into items that appeal to their interests and needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each audience, choose facts, tone, and presentation that will resonate (e.g., give jewelers information about amber; give sports fans data on Lithuanian sports; give senators legislative-relevant facts). Use language, format and channels appropriate to each subgroup. This increases receptivity and practical influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert substantive material into newsworthy stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Make accurate studies and treatises into interesting stories of news value rather than merely issuing dry treatises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit, dramatize, and package research or scholarly material so editors and the public will publish and read it. Example: Roumania—turned historically correct studies into news stories that attracted public interest; magazine features made the basis of inquiries and press coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third-party authority: endorsements, experts, and surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize on the authority of impartial experts, surveys or respected figures to lend credibility and make claims acceptable to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission or publicize surveys, obtain endorsements, have physicians or other experts conduct inquiries, and disseminate collated results via press and organizations. Examples: bacon campaign used a physician’s survey to recommend hearty breakfasts; trade magazine used symposium answers collated and sent to newspapers, and Herbert Hoover’s commendation amplified an article's reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide positive evidence/actions rather than mere denial
rubrics_metrics.description: To counter rumors or damaging impressions, give the public positive evidence of contrary intentions rather than rely on denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design concrete actions that demonstrably contradict the rumor (e.g., immediately renew a prominent employee’s long-term contract and announce it instead of just denying closure). Positive, demonstrable acts are harder to discredit than denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan coordinated multi-channel campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple and overlapping avenues of approach—mass meetings, petitions, lectures, advertising, radio, motion pictures, mail, press relations—to build sustained public awareness and pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map campaign phases, sequence actions for cumulative effect, and coordinate timing and content across channels. Example: Lithuania campaign combined exhaustive research, targeted materials, mass meetings, petitions, delegations to Congress, press corrections, advertising, radio, and films to change awareness and official attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize and stage events to create publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Create and publicize ceremonies or highly visual events which carry desired implications to the public and press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan symbolic, photo- and telegraph-friendly events (launchings, inaugurations, ceremonial firsts) involving notable figures to generate news and images that reinforce the message. Examples: Piave ship launching with prominent Italians and telegraphed messages to Italy; inter-city radio inauguration with mayors exchanging first messages; Metropolitan Opera performance representing national groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opinion leaders and group leaders to influence wider publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Make leaders of clubs, professions, business associations and other organized groups articulate opinions that will influence their constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and recruit respected local or national leaders (e.g., clubwomen, business associations, religious leaders) to issue statements, participate in events, or distribute materials. Examples: club women surveyed to influence hair fashion; Fifth Avenue Association's coordinated action to encourage employers to rehire ex-servicemen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze public attitudes via research and inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Study literature, interview representatives of groups, and conduct market and opinion inquiries to discover root causes of attitudes and reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews, surveys, literature review and field inquiry before designing interventions. Example: analysis of New York's reputation as 'cold and inhospitable' involved talking to visitors and representatives, examining literature and attacks, then forming the Welcome Stranger Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor medium and format to the message and client
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose among telegraph, circular, advertising, book publication, exhibits, or scholarships depending on the client’s objective and the public to be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not one medium or tactic fits all clients or messages. Consider audience expectations and reputational effects—e.g., some stores should use price advertising, others should not; one client may need a book, another an exhibit; one should found scholarships to influence academic opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize on existing content and re-distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify valuable existing editorial content and amplify its reach through abstracts, syndication, reprints and distribution to specialized journals and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find underused editorial material and repurpose it: collate responses from influential people, create abstracts for press release, distribute to class journals and associations for reprinting. Example: magazine article about 'the pace that kills' used a physician-led inquiry and abstracts to reach influential readers and advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create unified, non‑partisan coalitions when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Form non-partisan committees that bring together diverse groups to present seemingly disinterested and unified public support for an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit representatives from across political, social and professional spectra to create a single visible voice (example: forming a non-partisan committee of women for the League of Nations) to reflect broad support and reduce partisan attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage timing and synchronization for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coordinated timing—holiday dates, symbolic days, synchronized displays—to amplify visibility and create associative meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange simultaneous displays or events (e.g., Bastille Day citation displays) and choose occasions with symbolic resonance to gain editorial and public attention and to capitalize on pre-existing news cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure effectiveness by observable public responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate campaigns by tangible changes in public behavior or attitudes (e.g., cancellations ceased, wheat harvest labor obtained, increased readership or sales interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track concrete outcomes (reservations restored, labor recruited within days, rediscovered magazine prestige) as primary indicators of campaign success; use press pickup, official actions, and distribution metrics as proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize crowd and group psychology in shaping opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is largely formed by group/herd mechanisms; new ideas must be accepted by groups, not just individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design appeals that address group identities, use social proof and leaders, and anticipate defensive reactions (e.g., labeling dissent as 'propaganda'). Understand that advocacy seen as education by one group may be deemed propaganda by another; craft strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain ethical standards; refuse harmful retainers
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel must judge the social and ethical results of his work and refuse clients or retainers which would propagate unsocial or harmful movements; 'he must never accept a retainer or assume a position which puts his duty to the groups he represents above his duty to his own standards of integrity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt internal standards akin to a professional code: scrutinize prospective clients for social utility, avoid advocacy that undermines public welfare, refuse work whose consequences are ethically unacceptable. Balance client loyalty with duty to larger society; use ethical judgment as a screening mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tangible proofs and demonstrable benefits to influence skeptical publics
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming benefits (dietetic, economic, social), back assertions by demonstrable facts, studies and organized distribution so claims can be independently assessed and spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ medical surveys, expert-backed inquiries and reproducible data; distribute abstracts and reports to trustworthy outlets; aim to have organizations reprint and disseminate findings so claims seem less like partisan spin. Example: radium bank to make radium available and the physician-backed bacon health claims.
